summary: Reviewed 2 files (APIKeyMethodInterface.php, APIKeyMethodTrait.php). 0 Critical, 0 High, 1 Medium (phased-rollout interim state noted — by design), 1 Low (non-final trait method), 1 Info. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed. Security sign-off: PASS.

comments.note: A01 — Broken Access Control (phased rollout): The null default in APIKeyMethodTrait means all 20 HCP Editor API methods will silently skip the user-rights check until they are updated in Step 7 (WP-00X). If the authorize() enforcement gate (WP-003) deploys before the HCP Editor right overrides (Step 7), every method passes the user-rights branch with null. This is the intended incremental rollout design and is explicitly documented in the plan, but the window between WP-003 and Step 7 must be kept short in production to avoid a rights-check gap. No immediate vulnerability, but track as operational risk.

A01 — Broken Access Control (non-final trait method): getRequiredRight() in APIKeyMethodTrait is public and non-final, meaning any subclass can override it to return null even after a specific right has been assigned in a parent class. This is intentional by design (overrides are the mechanism for per-method rights), but there is no enforcement preventing an override from weakening a parent's non-null right back to null. Recommend documenting in the trait that overrides should only strengthen, not weaken, the right declaration.

A09 — Security Logging: The PHPDoc on getRequiredRight() in APIKeyMethodInterface correctly documents that the framework will enforce the right. However, the interface-level doc does not mention that enforcement failures will be logged internally (with the right name) but not exposed to callers. This is handled correctly in Step 5 (authorize() method per plan), but a cross-reference in the interface PHPDoc would help future implementors understand the security contract completely.

Info — No injection, cryptographic, SSRF, deserialization, or misconfiguration risks in scope. getRequiredRight() returns a string constant used as a rights identifier, not passed to any interpreter or SQL query within the two modified files. Type safety is enforced via declare(strict_types=1) and PHP's native ?string return type. The error constant values (183005, 183006) in APIMethodInterface are sequential, non-guessable, and set in WP-001. makeForbidden() correctly uses HTTP 403 via the framework's Connectors_ResponseCode constant, not a magic number.

The non-final vs. final distinction between getRequiredRight() and manageParamAPIKey() in the trait is architecturally correct: manageParamAPIKey() owns mutable $apiKeyHandler state (must not be overridden), while getRequiredRight() must remain overrideable for HCP Editor methods to declare specific rights in Step 7.

comments.note: Pattern alignment with AllowableMigrationInterface is strong. The new getRequiredRight(): ?string on APIKeyMethodInterface mirrors AllowableMigrationInterface::getRequiredRight(): ?string exactly — same method name, same return type, same null semantics. Developers familiar with the admin screen pattern will understand the API rights pattern immediately.

[documentation-forward] APIKeyMethodTrait::getRequiredRight() has no method-level docblock. The Security Auditor noted that overrides should only strengthen, not weaken, a parent's non-null right declaration. A brief docblock on the trait method (or an @inheritdoc with an added note about strengthening-only overrides) would make this constraint discoverable for future implementors without reading the interface PHPDoc. The interface itself is thorough; the trait implementation is the entry point developers will most likely override.

Minor PHPDoc style observation (non-blocking): AllowableMigrationInterface uses @return string|NULL (uppercase) while the new interface uses @return string|null (lowercase). The new lowercase form is idiomatic modern PHP. No action needed — just noting the style divergence between the two files for awareness.
